strengths: Novel and well-motivated central question — challenging the common intuition that depth alone drives MIA resistance in collaborative inference, supported by concrete empirical counterexamples on ViT, ResNet, and IR-152 before the theoretical analysis is even introduced.

Rigorous information-theoretic derivation (entropy upper bounds via maximum-entropy Gaussian and determinant-trace inequality, full proofs in Appendix A) linking the H(X|Z) lower bound to an interpretable quantity R²_c, and an honest treatment of the differential-to-discrete entropy bridge under finite precision (Appendix B-C), including explicit acknowledgment that the correction term κ_Δ(m) can be loose.

Extensive empirical validation spanning four architectures (IR-152, ResNet-50, VGG19, ViT) and multiple datasets (CIFAR-10, FaceScrub, KMNIST/MNIST/EMNIST), with consistent findings that dimension-matched deeper layers do not guarantee resistance, supporting the representational-transition thesis.

Practical contributions beyond pure theory: an automatic GPZ-locating algorithm (Algorithm 1) with dimension normalization and stability checks (across sampling seeds, training seeds, and LS condition), plus a thorough deployment-overhead analysis (latency, communication, memory, energy) that connects the theoretical findings to real deployment tradeoffs.

Multiple stress tests of the core claim: entropy-enhancement ablations (FFT, normalization, NN-based) and inversion-model-enhancement ablations (attention variants) both show decision-level representations remain comparatively robust, strengthening the causal story rather than relying on a single fixed attacker.
Code availability is mentioned (GitHub links for model/training and inversion architecture), aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central theoretical bound is explicitly acknowledged to be potentially 'numerically loose' and can become 'vacuous in absolute value' once the finite-precision correction κ_Δ(m) is included; the qualitative ordering argument (via data-processing inequality) partially compensates, but this materially weakens claims that the bound is directly actionable rather than a coarse indicator.

The 'Neural Vortex' concept, presented as a headline contribution in the abstract/intro, is explicitly downgraded in the appendix (Sec. G) to 'only an intuitive interpretation... not a standalone formal mechanism,' which creates a tension between how prominently it is marketed in the main text versus its actual epistemic status.

No direct quantitative comparison against existing published defenses (noise injection, information bottleneck methods, PATROL, PrivaScissors, etc.) is provided; the paper explicitly frames this as out of scope ('the appropriate evaluation is theory validity... rather than head-to-head comparison'), but this makes it hard for readers to judge how GPZ-based partitioning compares to the privacy-utility tradeoffs of prior defenses it critiques.

The active-location algorithm is validated on only two architectures (IR-152, VGG19) in Table 5, and the claimed post-hoc/active duality is somewhat circular—MIA outcomes are still needed to confirm the located zone is correct, softening the 'deployment-oriented guidance' claim.

Scope is restricted to vision/CNN and one small ViT configuration; the extension to Transformers/text is explicitly left as a 'cautious hypothesis' for future work, limiting the generality of the findings despite claims of broad applicability implied by 'collaborative inference' framing.

Reported aggregate numbers (4× MSE increase, 66% stronger resistance) are averages over multiple settings without variance/confidence intervals in the main text, and the extensive appendix tables (though detailed) are not accompanied by statistical significance testing across repeated runs for the headline results.

The overall presentation is extremely dense, with substantial reliance on ~37 pages of appendix for core proofs and even for some central experimental interpretation (e.g., R²_c evolution visualizations only qualitatively discussed via t-SNE in Fig. 3 without a quantitative trend plot in the main text).

strengths: Addresses an interesting and underexplored upstream question for collaborative inference privacy: where to partition rather than how to perturb, which is a useful reframing relative to the noise/bottleneck defence literature.

Substantial theoretical effort: differential-entropy upper bounds for feature- vs. decision-level representations, a finite-precision discretization bridge, and first-order analysis of how one-hot vs. label-smoothed training reshapes the intra-class radius R_c^2, all with detailed (if lengthy) appendix proofs.

Reasonably broad empirical coverage across four architectures (IR-152, ResNet-50, VGG19, ViT) and multiple data types (natural images, faces, handwritten scripts), including stress tests with enhanced entropy and stronger inversion-model attention mechanisms.
Practical deployment-overhead analysis (latency, communication payload, energy, EDP/ED2P) adds some applied value beyond the theory, offering a lens for trading off resistance against edge cost.

Several concrete, falsifiable observations (e.g., ViT's persistent patch tokens preventing transition, ResNet residual connections delaying it) that are intuitive and consistent with the Markov/data-processing-inequality argument.
weaknesses: The central entropy bounds are loose surrogate upper bounds (Gaussian maximum-entropy, determinant-trace inequality) whose resulting 'lower bound' on H(X|Z) is explicitly acknowledged to be potentially vacuous (Appendix C); the connection between this qualitative bound-gap (Eq. 8) and the empirically observed abrupt MSE jump is asserted rather than tightly proven, so the theory functions more as post-hoc rationalization than a predictive guarantee.

The 'Neural Vortex' concept, prominently featured in the title/abstract/contributions, is explicitly described by the authors themselves as 'not a standalone formal mechanism' and merely an 'analysis-backed explanatory concept'/metaphor (Appendix G uses a stirred-liquid analogy). Presenting a self-admittedly informal heuristic as a headline contribution risks overclaiming.

The Golden Partition Zone localization procedure (R_c^2 drop with an empirically chosen 20% threshold, ad hoc dimension normalization) is tuned to match empirically observed transition points (Table 5), making the validation partly circular: the paper both defines GPZ via R_c^2 and validates R_c^2 by checking it matches where MIA outcomes change, rather than demonstrating independent predictive power on unseen architectures a priori.

The ViT case already undermines the generality of the 'depth enables transition' narrative: patch-token behavior oscillates and the explanation ('alternating influence of self-attention') is offered post hoc without a mechanism tied back to the R_c^2 theory, suggesting the framework may not transfer cleanly beyond CNN-style architectures.

No direct quantitative comparison against existing defence baselines (noise injection, information bottleneck methods such as Xia et al. 2025 or PATROL pruning) in terms of resistance-utility trade-off, despite these being the natural competitors; the paper explicitly places this out of scope, which limits the demonstrated practical significance of the proposed partitioning guidance.

Attack evaluation relies on a fixed family of inversion architectures (enhanced CNN decoders with attention), not fully adaptive attacks specifically optimized against GPZ splits (e.g., generative/diffusion-based attacks mentioned in related work), so claims of '66% stronger resistance under stronger inversion models' may not hold against more adversarially tailored attackers.

The headline aggregate statistics (4x MSE increase, 66% resistance gain) are drawn from a specific, fairly narrow set of architecture/dataset/attack configurations and risk being overgeneralized in the abstract relative to the more nuanced and sometimes contradictory per-architecture results in the appendix (e.g., Table 7 shows non-monotonic behavior within fixed-dimension blocks).

The manuscript is heavily back-loaded with ~27 pages of appendix math relative to a 9-page main text, which raises concerns about whether the formal apparatus substantively drives the empirical findings or is largely decorative; core experimental conclusions in the main text remain qualitative and descriptive.

Reproducibility is only partially verifiable: code/GitHub links are referenced but not concretely provided in the manuscript text, and hyperparameter/threshold choices (e.g., τ, dimension normalization scheme) that affect GPZ localization are introduced without sensitivity analysis beyond limited stability checks.

strengths: Novel reframing of the MIA-defense problem: instead of proposing another shallow-layer perturbation defense, the paper asks the upstream question of where to partition a model for intrinsic resistance, which is a useful conceptual shift for the CI privacy literature.

Rigorous information-theoretic derivation connecting conditional entropy H(X|Z) lower bounds to the intra-class mean-squared radius R_c^2, with detailed and largely self-contained appendix proofs (maximum entropy principle, determinant-trace inequality, finite-precision discretization bridge from differential to Shannon entropy).

Extensive empirical validation across four distinct architectures (IR-152, ResNet-50, VGG19, ViT) and multiple datasets (CIFAR-10, FaceScrub, KMNIST/MNIST/EMNIST), directly testing and falsifying the common 'depth alone helps' intuition with concrete counterexamples (e.g., ViT, ResNet blocks with unchanged or worsening inversion resistance at increasing depth).

Thorough stress-testing of the central claim via multiple independent attack-strengthening strategies (FFT/normalization/NN-based entropy enhancement of Z, and progressively stronger inversion architectures with attention mechanisms), showing the decision-level resistance persists under adaptive attackers.

Practical, quantitative deployment-overhead analysis (latency, communication payload, memory, energy, EDP/ED2P) that connects the theoretical partition criterion to actionable system-level tradeoffs for real CI deployment.

Reasonably transparent about scope and limitations, explicitly noting that the GPZ may not emerge in architectures that persistently retain patch/token-level information (ViT) and that extension to text/sequence domains is speculative future work.

Reproducibility aids: detailed pseudocode (Algorithm 1) for actively locating the GPZ via R_c^2, with stability checks (sampling, training-seed, label-smoothing condition) and a stated public code release.
weaknesses: The core theoretical result chains several loose upper bounds (max-entropy Gaussian surrogate, determinant-trace/AM-GM inequality) and argues the resulting gap is 'typically' or 'sizeable' positive (Eq. 8) rather than providing a tight or universally guaranteed inequality; the practical tightness of the derived H(X|Z) lower bound is not empirically validated against actual measured mutual information or entropy.

The 'Golden Partition Zone' criterion is only actionable in hindsight or via post-hoc layer-wise scanning of R_c^2/MIA outcomes; the paper's own discussion concedes that for some architectures (ViT) no clear GPZ emerges at all, which weakens the generality and practical utility of the proposed localization method as a deployment tool compared to simply running MIA empirically.

'Neural Vortex' is explicitly flagged by the authors as a metaphorical/explanatory concept rather than a formal mechanism, and Appendix G's liquid-vortex analogy, while honest, offers limited additional predictive or quantitative value beyond the already-derived R_c^2 training dynamics (Appendix E/F); this raises a question of whether the terminology primarily serves branding rather than new insight beyond known label-smoothing/representation-contraction effects.

Headline quantitative claims (4x MSE increase, 66% stronger resistance) are aggregated/representative numbers from a fairly small set of architectures and 64x64-resolution datasets; it is unclear how robust these specific percentages are to model scale, resolution, or task type, limiting confidence in generalizability to larger, production-scale CI deployments.

No direct empirical comparison against existing shallow-layer perturbation or information-bottleneck defenses in terms of resulting privacy-utility trade-off, even though the related-work section positions the paper as complementary; this makes it hard to assess the comparative significance of GPZ-based partitioning versus established baselines.

The paper is very dense, with the bulk of the rigorous derivation and many key validation experiments (ResNet-50 results, overhead tables, stability checks) relegated to a lengthy appendix; the main text alone leaves some claims (e.g., the gap argument, the practical algorithm's reliability) under-supported without consulting extensive supplementary material.
